title: Your Gut Bacteria May Explain Why Coffee Wrecks Your Sleep — and a 7,000-Person Study Just Mapped the Connection
excerpt: A Nature Communications study of nearly 7,000 Dutch adults found 137 bacterial species linked to sleep quality. Two Clostridia species appear to mediate coffee's effect on social jet lag — the gap between your weekday and weekend sleep clocks.
body:
Most people know that coffee keeps you up. Fewer realise that the reason may not be caffeine alone — but the bacteria living in your gut. A large-scale study published in *Nature Communications* has traced a direct biological pathway from your coffee cup, through specific gut microbes, to the disruption of your internal clock.

The research, based on 6,941 participants in the Lifelines Dutch Microbiome Project, is one of the largest studies to date examining the three-way relationship between sleep, diet and the gut microbiome. Its findings suggest that targeted interventions — dietary changes, probiotics, or even adjusting when you drink coffee — could improve sleep in ways that simply "cutting back on caffeine" cannot.

## 137 Species Tied to How You Sleep

The research team analysed stool samples alongside detailed sleep questionnaires covering sleep quality, chronotype (whether you are a morning or evening person), sleep duration and social jet lag — the mismatch between your body's preferred sleep schedule and the one your work week imposes.

They identified 137 bacterial species whose abundance was statistically associated with at least one sleep characteristic. Of these, 35.6% were independently validated in a separate cohort, lending unusual confidence to the results. The associations held after adjusting for diet, physical activity, BMI, alcohol use and medication.

Lower microbial diversity — fewer types of bacteria in the gut — was consistently linked to poorer sleep quality, a later chronotype and greater social jet lag. Beta diversity, which measures the variation in gut composition between individuals, was also tied to sleep quality and social jet lag.



> **"Its findings suggest that targeted interventions — dietary changes, probiotics, or even adjusting when you drink coffee — could improve sleep in ways that simply "cutting back on caffeine" cannot."**


## The Coffee-Gut-Clock Pathway

The study's most striking finding came from mediation analysis, a statistical technique that tests whether one factor acts as a middleman between two others. Two species of Clostridia bacteria — identified as UC5_1_1E11 and SGB14844 — appeared to sit squarely in the pathway between coffee consumption and social jet lag.

Here's how it works: higher coffee intake boosted the abundance of these two Clostridia species. In turn, greater levels of those species were associated with more severe social jet lag — meaning bigger gaps between workday and free-day sleep timing. The relationship held across three different directional models the researchers tested, strengthening the case that these bacteria are genuine mediators, not bystanders.

This doesn't mean coffee is universally bad for sleep. It means the effect of coffee on your circadian rhythm may depend, in part, on the composition of your gut microbiome. Two people drinking the same amount of espresso could experience very different sleep outcomes based on their microbial profile.

## What Changes in Species Abundance Actually Mean

The study also used a clever analytical approach to tease apart cause and effect. Through mediation networks incorporating diet, they found that most changes in microbial species abundance were a *consequence* of sleep behaviour — not a cause. In other words, sleeping poorly reshapes your gut more than your gut disrupts your sleep.

But a critical subset of species worked the other way. The two Clostridia species, for instance, appeared to mediate diet's influence on sleep — suggesting that what you eat can alter your gut in ways that then change how you sleep. This opens a therapeutic door: if specific bacteria amplify coffee's circadian-disrupting effects, targeting those bacteria (through diet, prebiotics or probiotics) could mitigate the damage without requiring you to give up your morning cup.

## The South Asian Angle

The implications are particularly relevant for the Indian diaspora. South Asians are among the world's heaviest tea and coffee consumers — India alone consumes over 250,000 tonnes of coffee annually, and chai culture ensures caffeine is a fixture from morning to evening. Meanwhile, NRI professionals in tech, healthcare and finance frequently work across time zones, compounding social jet lag.

Emerging research has also shown that the South Asian gut microbiome differs meaningfully from that of European and East Asian populations, shaped by dietary patterns rich in lentils, fermented foods like idli and dosa batter, and spice-heavy preparations. Whether these differences make South Asians more or less susceptible to the coffee-Clostridia-sleep pathway is an open question — but one that the study's framework now makes testable.

For anyone whose evening coffee seems to hit harder than it used to, the answer may not be willpower. It may be in your gut.

*Sources: Nature Communications (2026), DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-68791-9; Lifelines Dutch Microbiome Project; Nature Communications (2026), Boscaini et al., "Habitual coffee intake shapes the gut microbiome and modifies host physiology and cognition."*
